    └─
      seems like OP overrelies on AI, more than a tool they believe it to be a credible source of fresh information, and this is a mindset we have to combat.

      as someone whose research has been in probing the limits of AI models' reasoning capabilities, i'm confident in saying that AI is not qualified to be something we bounce our ideas off of. it always wants to please, it generalises, spits out only popular knowledge, it evades straight answers when something more niche is asked of it. you should bounce questions off of students, professors, other academics. AI will train you to want correct answers and want them immediately, and that training will be done in a totally antisocial environment. it does not prepare you to be a successful engineer and a generation of students isolated and coddled in their AI-response mindset will be incredibly detrimental to our society. i appreciate your skepticism but we need to be more anti-AI.

┌─ COMMENT ID: ncj7sk5
│  AUTHOR: veryunwisedecisions
│  DATE: 2025-09-05T16:11:48
│  UPVOTES: 2
└─
  I do read them. I try to read multiple at a time, since different textbooks approach concepts with more or less rigor depending on the intent of the textbook. 

  For example, Boylestad teaches you about electronic devices in a "let's approximate stuff" way, and through a fair amount of examples it shows to you that, for practical purposes, the approximations that it teaches you are good enough. Millman, however, and for the same subjects, likes to go a bit more into the math and the physics of electronic devices, not giving you as-much examples, being more theory-heavy than practical; it feels like it talks to you like you already know what you're doing and only need to check some details, whereas Boylestad feels like it talks to you like if you were an actual student.

  But both styles are appreciated, because when you have both options, you have both depth and practicality, which will show in your exams, probably.

┌─ COMMENT ID: ncj4a9m
│  AUTHOR: polymath_uk
│  DATE: 2025-09-05T15:41:40
│  UPVOTES: 4
└─
  The problem with most textbooks is that they're written by experts (yeah - I know that sounds like a ridiculous statement). But the reason that this is a problem is that the author often assumes the reader also has 20 years experience in the field and thus has a comprehensive context into which to place the new information. But students of a subject don't, by definition, have that context. So the reader is left with a bunch of highly complex theory that sits in complete isolation, so the only way to 'learn it' is to simply try to memorise these disparate facts, and the only way to use them is to look through for an example problem that at least vaguely resembles the problem set in class and then attempt to deduce any connections.

  Good textbooks, in my opinion, have titles that start with "An introduction to..." or "A beginners guide to" because they start from where you actually are: the beginning. Electronics engineers will understand what I mean when I describe this problem as an "impedance mismatch".

  Source: I'm an academic.

  ┌─ COMMENT ID: ncj66j5
  │  AUTHOR: veryunwisedecisions
  │  DATE: 2025-09-05T15:58:06
  │  UPVOTES: 2
  └─
    Well, textbooks are recommended to you by professors as you go through the curriculum. So, they assume you have some sort of understanding of the concepts that the textbook will use to teach you new stuff, since you already meet the prerequisites for that class if you're in it.

    For example, an engineering electromagnetics textbook will assume you have knowledge of maths up to calc 3 and some, and communicate concepts using that math; so, the electrogmanetism professor will recommend you that book because they know you know calc 3 already. The textbook isn't going to teach you calculus from scratch, that's what the calculus courses were for. By that point, you should be familiar with calculus already.

    But I've never taken post-graduate courses. I assume the textbooks for those are, on average, much more complex. I imagine it's because everyone in there assumes you know what they're talking about, since you're there because you met the prerequisites to be there. So they hit you with stuff that they think is on your level.

    ┌─ COMMENT ID: ncj9cud
    │  AUTHOR: polymath_uk
    │  DATE: 2025-09-05T16:24:13
    │  UPVOTES: 3
    └─
      I get what you're saying and I agree largely. But beyond undergraduate degrees, textbooks are essentially not useful (somewhat useful at MSc level). The idea of for example a PhD is that it's an original and substantial contribution to human knowledge. It's not a learn from books and take a test process. The point of it is to develop new knowledge and publish that new knowledge via the academic publishing system. Some of that, if it stands the test of time, is what ends up appearing in textbooks. The difference between working at undergrad level from textbooks vs working at doctoral level from contemporary papers is absolutely brutal. Like, having to look up the meaning of words in every sentence of the paper brutal in some cases, and you will be expected to cite at least 150 papers in a thesis just as the literature review chapter, let alone your own original contribution.

      I think academics get used to working at that level and forget what being a complete beginner is like - hence the impedance problem I mentioned before.

┌─ COMMENT ID: ncj66j5
│  AUTHOR: veryunwisedecisions
│  DATE: 2025-09-05T15:58:06
│  UPVOTES: 2
└─
  Well, textbooks are recommended to you by professors as you go through the curriculum. So, they assume you have some sort of understanding of the concepts that the textbook will use to teach you new stuff, since you already meet the prerequisites for that class if you're in it.

  For example, an engineering electromagnetics textbook will assume you have knowledge of maths up to calc 3 and some, and communicate concepts using that math; so, the electrogmanetism professor will recommend you that book because they know you know calc 3 already. The textbook isn't going to teach you calculus from scratch, that's what the calculus courses were for. By that point, you should be familiar with calculus already.

  But I've never taken post-graduate courses. I assume the textbooks for those are, on average, much more complex. I imagine it's because everyone in there assumes you know what they're talking about, since you're there because you met the prerequisites to be there. So they hit you with stuff that they think is on your level.

  ┌─ COMMENT ID: ncj9cud
  │  AUTHOR: polymath_uk
  │  DATE: 2025-09-05T16:24:13
  │  UPVOTES: 3
  └─
    I get what you're saying and I agree largely. But beyond undergraduate degrees, textbooks are essentially not useful (somewhat useful at MSc level). The idea of for example a PhD is that it's an original and substantial contribution to human knowledge. It's not a learn from books and take a test process. The point of it is to develop new knowledge and publish that new knowledge via the academic publishing system. Some of that, if it stands the test of time, is what ends up appearing in textbooks. The difference between working at undergrad level from textbooks vs working at doctoral level from contemporary papers is absolutely brutal. Like, having to look up the meaning of words in every sentence of the paper brutal in some cases, and you will be expected to cite at least 150 papers in a thesis just as the literature review chapter, let alone your own original contribution.

    I think academics get used to working at that level and forget what being a complete beginner is like - hence the impedance problem I mentioned before.

└─
  seems like OP overrelies on AI, more than a tool they believe it to be a credible source of fresh information, and this is a mindset we have to combat.

  as someone whose research has been in probing the limits of AI models' reasoning capabilities, i'm confident in saying that AI is not qualified to be something we bounce our ideas off of. it always wants to please, it generalises, spits out only popular knowledge, it evades straight answers when something more niche is asked of it. you should bounce questions off of students, professors, other academics. AI will train you to want correct answers and want them immediately, and that training will be done in a totally antisocial environment. it does not prepare you to be a successful engineer and a generation of students isolated and coddled in their AI-response mindset will be incredibly detrimental to our society. i appreciate your skepticism but we need to be more anti-AI.

    email is a method of communication from human to human. AI averages the data it's been fed and regurgitates what it knows will please you (edit: sp.). if you are trying to do anything more than, for instance, basic thermodynamics (the kind of things explained to death on blogs, forum posts, publicly available resources), it will feed you generalisations or flat out incorrect facts and data. even if it fed you a stream of perfectly correct responses, you would not be learning, you wouldn't be challenging yourself! this isn't a case of "get with the times," awareness needs raised that AI 1. does not understand so 2. must not teach.

    source: my work for the past few months has been in probing the reasoning capabilities of AI models. they are piss poor!

└─
  I was in the Air Force for 4 years from 2011-2015. Im not the most qualified person in the world, but I could shed a bit of insight. 

   Going in after college is the move imo. You can commission as an officer better pay, housing, jobs treatment, and you're gonna be in what is basically a manager position almost right away after training.

   Don't fucking enlist if you have a degree. Go the officer route. 

  You'll definitely still have a promising career when you get out. You'll have an engineering degree, 4 years military experience as a commissioned officer, youll have leadership experience out the ass plus whatever experience you get for your job. There are engineering positions in the military. I dont know exactly what it entails but they will most likely try to utilize your engineering degree. 

   Im assuming SF you mean special forces. You need to be in like really really fucking good shape. You're going to get hurt, shot at and probably watch some of your friends die. You might die. Its not a joke or a decision to be made lightly and they will break your fucking soul to make sure youre the right person for the job. Special forces are the highest level of professional war fighter the military has to offer. Alot of times special forces washouts get shoved into whatever job they need filled and you have little to no say in what happens. Im not trying to discourage you im trying to be as honest as I can. Just some things to consider. 

   Personally, if i could rewind the clock and put myself in ur shoes? I'd join the Air Force to be a pilot. All of the things I said in the previous paragraph apply to becoming a pilot but to a lesser degree. You gotta be in shape. it's dangerous as hell and the standards and expectations are sky high. You'd get relatively nice facilities compared to other branches as far as base ammetaties go (Gyms, chow halls, grocery stores, etc are generally nicer on AF bases). Pilots get to travel the world, they still get to do some spicy things that could scratch the itch your desire to be Sf is giving you. Being a pilot with an engineering degree would also open doors to work as an aerospace engineer after the military. The pilot thing is what I would do if I wanted maximum excitement and opportunity to do cool stuff and travel the world without so much risk of being in direct combat. Flight school is also very difficult and a larger time commitment than other military careers. 

   The air force also has boots on the ground special forces if youre still wanting that route (PJs are some of the baddest Mfers on the planet you should check them out)

  Whatever you decide. You're gonna be fine either way. Go in do your 4 years, get the benis, and split or make it a career youll be set up for success either way. 

  Joining the military was the best thing I ever did. The only thing I would change is I would have gotten a degree first and not go in as enlisted. If you have any more questions, feel free to ask or dm me, and I'll try do my best to help. 

   All of this is coming from someone who has been disconnected from that life for a while so take it with a grain of salt but I didnt see any other answers. Good luck with school and whatever you decide youll be fine. ✌️

┌─ COMMENT ID: nci5hcz
│  AUTHOR: Electrical_Grape_559
│  DATE: 2025-09-05T10:16:43
│  UPVOTES: 5
└─
  You won’t be doing that math on the job. We have software for that. Besides, many engineers find that they don’t even enjoy doing design work.

  A BSEET is an applied science degree. A BSEE is a theoretical science degree. Want to build electronics using existing technology? The BSEET will get you there. Want to work in a physics lab pushing the limits of technology? Better get that BSEE.

  Important to note: a BSEET is NOT a technician degree in the U.S. If you want to be a technician, an AS is all you need.

  Source: my title has been “electrical engineer” (or some derivation thereof) at several different employers since i graduated with a BSEET over a decade ago.

  PM me if you more info, redditors seem to have a thing against legitimate, accredited, BSEET degrees. Part of the confusion is due to societal differences, and another part is ignorance.

  If you have the capability to finish it, do it. Hands on. Now is the time and down the line you will probably regret not finishing it. 

  You can ALWAYS go work as a highly skilled technician if you go to a trade school after. If hands on is what you like.

  The other way around is, well, much more frustrating.

  (Words of a 28 yo. who should have done it this way and now is back in college for EE). 

  Believe me, the sooner you get your EE, the better of you are to do whatever the hell you like with you career. Otherwise at some moment you'll feel stucked or greatly slowed down because of that piece of paper (and knowledge).

┌─ COMMENT ID: nclgzy2
│  AUTHOR: Lk1738
│  DATE: 2025-09-05T23:29:20
│  UPVOTES: 1
└─
  Technology degrees are for people with working experience to either be competitive at work, or to obtain an ABET degree that allows them to get into (real) engineering.

  Your tech degree will only help you get entry level technician work, where youll mostly be under qualified due to not getting hands on experience at a vocational school.

  I have a tech degree, and still had to complete Calculus 1, Calc 2, linear algebra, and a python course (2 programming classes, 1 had to be more advanced than intro to programming.) Tech degrees that do not require these courses are most likely not ABET accredited, and imo are a waste of time and money.

  If you’re 19 in college, pursue an engineering degree. 

  This is specific to the US, although I think my recommendation is valid for Canadians too.

TITLE: Internship offer

POST CONTENT:
Hi guys, I've been applying to spring internships and just got my first offer today. I have an interview with a company I really like on Monday and was wondering how I should go about this? 

Should I mention that I have an offer in my interview on monday to try to apply some pressure. Also would it be bad to still be applying to jobs to see if I get a potentially better offer? 

I haven't had any experience with this so any advice would be much appreciated.

┌─ COMMENT ID: nchqmjr
│  AUTHOR: lRedBaronl
│  DATE: 2025-09-05T08:33:52
│  UPVOTES: 3
└─
  I've been generally recommended not to mention other offers unless its extremely urgent (and I mean emergency emergency and you have a good rapport with the HM or HR). Your first interview should really be about showing why you're a good fit to them and tell them what makes a good fit for you. If your internship offer is on a timeline, I recommend asking them for an extension as its typically more appropriate there to discuss the situation of multiple offers (just allude to it). But really, go into your interview as separated from your other offer as possible except for weighing the options in your mind, otherwise, you may end up losing the possibility of a second offer entirely.

└─
  I applied externally without knowing anyone to help me get in the door. It’s taken multiple applications to get an offer. My best tips are: 
  1. apply to jobs that are recently posted. Like within the day. 
  2. Tailor your resume to the posting as much as you can but still being truthful about it. 
  3. If you do get an interview, practice STAR questions and remain confident. The whole goal is just making sure you’re a good fit. My first interview with them last year, I tanked the interview because I didn’t have a good response to one of the questions and I let it affect me to the point where it was downhill from there.

└─
  It does sacrifice depth but that doesn’t mean what most people think. If you look at both learning paths you will see that “more in depth ” really just means they take 1 class on each electrical engineering sub field(RF, Semiconductor, Power, and telecommunications) but all of those classes u could take as electives if u wanted. And when applying for jobs employers only care if you have experience in their specific area. They don’t care how much you know about RF, semiconductors and telecommunications if you don’t know anything about power. So just make sure to take the classes about the stuff you are interested in and you’ll be fine.

┌─ COMMENT ID: ncfsnf1

│  DATE: 2025-09-05T02:03:49
│  UPVOTES: 8
└─
  In my experience you're going to want to show some apititude in terms of applying the theory you're gonna learn. This is most common and perhaps effective in the form of an internship (some internships can be useless), but there are other forms you can look at if internships aren't available to you. You can really turn any of these into a good showcase of your abilities and interest: 

  \-- school design teams (AIAA DBF, Formula SAE, whatever your school has or you can start your own team in a recognized competition)

  \-- research in a lab on campus

  \-- personal projects, if your school has a makerspace that can be a great place to start, YouTube as well for inspiration. 

  Theres more ways I'm sure. Bottom line do something outside of class. Nothing wrong with an internship at a smaller local company. Definitely try to get one in. 

  Good luck! I started mechE at 26, about to finish at 29.

        └─
          4 month after first and second year for a total of 8 months, and then 4 months OR 16 months after third year (delay graduation by 2 semesters). This is very common at various schools in Canada, not just Waterloo (which requires 3x 4 month internships). The most common I find is 8-20 months, fail to find an internship after first year, but find a 4 month after second year, then do a full 16 months after third year which often leads to a full time job offer upon graduation. 

          I currently work in aerospace and we have plenty of mechanical interns.

      └─
        4 month after first and second year for a total of 8 months, and then 4 months OR 16 months after third year (delay graduation by 2 semesters). This is very common at various schools in Canada, not just Waterloo (which requires 3x 4 month internships). The most common I find is 8-20 months, fail to find an internship after first year, but find a 4 month after second year, then do a full 16 months after third year which often leads to a full time job offer upon graduation. 

        I currently work in aerospace and we have plenty of mechanical interns.

      └─
        4 month after first and second year for a total of 8 months, and then 4 months OR 16 months after third year (delay graduation by 2 semesters). This is very common at various schools in Canada, not just Waterloo (which requires 3x 4 month internships). The most common I find is 8-20 months, fail to find an internship after first year, but find a 4 month after second year, then do a full 16 months after third year which often leads to a full time job offer upon graduation. 

        I currently work in aerospace and we have plenty of mechanical interns.

        Up here some of the best engineering programs do require mandatory internship terms though like Waterloo, and that employer network they build is very strong because of that.

    └─
      4 month after first and second year for a total of 8 months, and then 4 months OR 16 months after third year (delay graduation by 2 semesters). This is very common at various schools in Canada, not just Waterloo (which requires 3x 4 month internships). The most common I find is 8-20 months, fail to find an internship after first year, but find a 4 month after second year, then do a full 16 months after third year which often leads to a full time job offer upon graduation. 

      I currently work in aerospace and we have plenty of mechanical interns.

      │  DATE: 2025-09-05T18:20:07
      │  UPVOTES: 1
      └─
        4 month after first and second year for a total of 8 months, and then 4 months OR 16 months after third year (delay graduation by 2 semesters). This is very common at various schools in Canada, not just Waterloo (which requires 3x 4 month internships). The most common I find is 8-20 months, fail to find an internship after first year, but find a 4 month after second year, then do a full 16 months after third year which often leads to a full time job offer upon graduation. 

        I currently work in aerospace and we have plenty of mechanical interns.

    ┌─ COMMENT ID: ncjqqww
    │  AUTHOR: ShadowBlades512
    │  DATE: 2025-09-05T18:20:07
    │  UPVOTES: 1
    └─
      4 month after first and second year for a total of 8 months, and then 4 months OR 16 months after third year (delay graduation by 2 semesters). This is very common at various schools in Canada, not just Waterloo (which requires 3x 4 month internships). The most common I find is 8-20 months, fail to find an internship after first year, but find a 4 month after second year, then do a full 16 months after third year which often leads to a full time job offer upon graduation. 

      I currently work in aerospace and we have plenty of mechanical interns.

    └─
      4 month after first and second year for a total of 8 months, and then 4 months OR 16 months after third year (delay graduation by 2 semesters). This is very common at various schools in Canada, not just Waterloo (which requires 3x 4 month internships). The most common I find is 8-20 months, fail to find an internship after first year, but find a 4 month after second year, then do a full 16 months after third year which often leads to a full time job offer upon graduation. 

      I currently work in aerospace and we have plenty of mechanical interns.

  │  DATE: 2025-09-05T18:20:07
  │  UPVOTES: 1
  └─
    4 month after first and second year for a total of 8 months, and then 4 months OR 16 months after third year (delay graduation by 2 semesters). This is very common at various schools in Canada, not just Waterloo (which requires 3x 4 month internships). The most common I find is 8-20 months, fail to find an internship after first year, but find a 4 month after second year, then do a full 16 months after third year which often leads to a full time job offer upon graduation. 

    I currently work in aerospace and we have plenty of mechanical interns.

      Up here some of the best engineering programs do require mandatory internship terms though like Waterloo, and that employer network they build is very strong because of that.

┌─ COMMENT ID: ncfx8f5
│  AUTHOR: LitRick6
│  DATE: 2025-09-05T02:25:47
│  UPVOTES: 2
└─
  Imo internships have 3 purposes. 2 of which you may have covered or can easily work on. The 3rd may take time/effort.

  1. Just the act of applying for internships will have you working on your resume, interview skills, networking, understanding application processes and when companies hire, etc. As someone who has already worked jobs, you might already have some of that down. You can also still network at career fairs, club/org events, etc with engineering recruiters throughout university even if youre not applying for internships. I do recommend networking throughout college instead of just waiting until your final semester to go to a career fair.

  2. Internships show you can work in a professional environment. Even if its not engineering, your previous experience may already cover this. Following dress codes, showing up to work on time, working on a team, reporting to a supervisor etc are generic work things that internships help show (especially if students dont have much work experience even in "basic" jobs like retail/fast food/etc). Also, internships can help show you've developed soft skills outside of just learning technical course material. Ie can you work on a team, can you do presentations, can you document stuff, can you work with customers, can you work with vendors, etc etc? Again, your previous job experience may already help cover this.

  3. Internships are also meant to show you can apply technical engineering knowledge to real world tasks outside of class. You said your previous work experience isn't relevant, so this is where you may struggle. But when im recruiting, I also factor in personal projects, club/org projects, undergrad research, etc. I personally did undergrad research in a professor lab and did some design/build work alongside testing (actually got it to count as a course credit so sort of towing the line of "outside of class experience") and it really improved my odds when applying to internships and fulltime jobs. I work in aerospace, so things like joining a universities AIAA or ASME student org and working on their group projects is good technical experience i look for on a resume. So if you cant do internships, find ways you can show off your ability to apply what you learned in class.

┌─ COMMENT ID: ncg5g1r
│  AUTHOR: R0ck3tSc13nc3
│  DATE: 2025-09-05T03:07:50
│  UPVOTES: 2
└─
  Hey there, congrats on going back to college in your thirties, but guess what, engineering college is not what you think it is. Instead of actually teaching you how to do the job on the job, it's more like an expensive ticket you buy into the engineering carnival. The actual engineering work is only somewhat related to the education you get in college. You're going to learn real work on real jobs in real engineering by going to internships that are quality. So yes, you look significantly less attractive by not having related internships. Whether on campus research or joining clubs, you can help cover yourself if you don't have an internship by at least doing something engineering related. 

  The people we hire, we don't care if they have a 4.0 if they've never had a job, and never joined a club, they're probably the last people we talk to. If somebody has a 3.2, rebuilt a car, built a website, helped run the rocket club, had an internship or at least a job at McDonald's, they would be preferred over that 4.0 student. Engineering this job about doing, not just about book learning

      └─
        4 month after first and second year for a total of 8 months, and then 4 months OR 16 months after third year (delay graduation by 2 semesters). This is very common at various schools in Canada, not just Waterloo (which requires 3x 4 month internships). The most common I find is 8-20 months, fail to find an internship after first year, but find a 4 month after second year, then do a full 16 months after third year which often leads to a full time job offer upon graduation. 

        I currently work in aerospace and we have plenty of mechanical interns.

    └─
      4 month after first and second year for a total of 8 months, and then 4 months OR 16 months after third year (delay graduation by 2 semesters). This is very common at various schools in Canada, not just Waterloo (which requires 3x 4 month internships). The most common I find is 8-20 months, fail to find an internship after first year, but find a 4 month after second year, then do a full 16 months after third year which often leads to a full time job offer upon graduation. 

      I currently work in aerospace and we have plenty of mechanical interns.

    └─
      4 month after first and second year for a total of 8 months, and then 4 months OR 16 months after third year (delay graduation by 2 semesters). This is very common at various schools in Canada, not just Waterloo (which requires 3x 4 month internships). The most common I find is 8-20 months, fail to find an internship after first year, but find a 4 month after second year, then do a full 16 months after third year which often leads to a full time job offer upon graduation. 

      I currently work in aerospace and we have plenty of mechanical interns.

  │  DATE: 2025-09-05T18:20:07
  │  UPVOTES: 1
  └─
    4 month after first and second year for a total of 8 months, and then 4 months OR 16 months after third year (delay graduation by 2 semesters). This is very common at various schools in Canada, not just Waterloo (which requires 3x 4 month internships). The most common I find is 8-20 months, fail to find an internship after first year, but find a 4 month after second year, then do a full 16 months after third year which often leads to a full time job offer upon graduation. 

    I currently work in aerospace and we have plenty of mechanical interns.

    └─
      4 month after first and second year for a total of 8 months, and then 4 months OR 16 months after third year (delay graduation by 2 semesters). This is very common at various schools in Canada, not just Waterloo (which requires 3x 4 month internships). The most common I find is 8-20 months, fail to find an internship after first year, but find a 4 month after second year, then do a full 16 months after third year which often leads to a full time job offer upon graduation. 

      I currently work in aerospace and we have plenty of mechanical interns.

  ┌─ COMMENT ID: ncjqqww
  │  AUTHOR: ShadowBlades512
  │  DATE: 2025-09-05T18:20:07
  │  UPVOTES: 1
  └─
    4 month after first and second year for a total of 8 months, and then 4 months OR 16 months after third year (delay graduation by 2 semesters). This is very common at various schools in Canada, not just Waterloo (which requires 3x 4 month internships). The most common I find is 8-20 months, fail to find an internship after first year, but find a 4 month after second year, then do a full 16 months after third year which often leads to a full time job offer upon graduation. 

    I currently work in aerospace and we have plenty of mechanical interns.

      Interesting. Wasn't required for us at my alma mater either but it was extremely important to get the experience though, pretty much every serious engineering student was trying to get a big 1 year internship after 3rd year, as it was the best way to get a company to give a full time return offer after graduation.

  └─
    4 month after first and second year for a total of 8 months, and then 4 months OR 16 months after third year (delay graduation by 2 semesters). This is very common at various schools in Canada, not just Waterloo (which requires 3x 4 month internships). The most common I find is 8-20 months, fail to find an internship after first year, but find a 4 month after second year, then do a full 16 months after third year which often leads to a full time job offer upon graduation. 

    I currently work in aerospace and we have plenty of mechanical interns.

┌─ COMMENT ID: ncjqqww

│  UPVOTES: 1
└─
  4 month after first and second year for a total of 8 months, and then 4 months OR 16 months after third year (delay graduation by 2 semesters). This is very common at various schools in Canada, not just Waterloo (which requires 3x 4 month internships). The most common I find is 8-20 months, fail to find an internship after first year, but find a 4 month after second year, then do a full 16 months after third year which often leads to a full time job offer upon graduation. 

  I currently work in aerospace and we have plenty of mechanical interns.

┌─ COMMENT ID: nceqss4
│  AUTHOR: R0ck3tSc13nc3
│  DATE: 2025-09-04T22:59:42
│  UPVOTES: 7
└─
  Speaking as a highly experienced professional engineer now semi-retired and teaching about engineering at a college, I've learned a few things that might help you collapse your probability space and reduce the number of multiverses in your head 

  Data talks and bullshit walks. Get more data. And the best place to get the data is to try to find people who hold the jobs that you hope to hold, and interview them or job shadowing them 

  Look past college and actually look at the jobs you're in. What does the day-to-day life look like for the electrical engineering jobs versus the civil engineering jobs. 

  Let's assume you even stay in your basic bucket, the bucket for electrical engineering can be anything from giant power lines and working with power companies to working at a microelectronics factory. And the bucket for civil engineering, that's pretty broad also, everything from geotech and digging in the dirt, to doing traffic, the general site planning, and more. In that same civil engineer can go work in the mechanical roles in aerospace, I've worked with plenty of them at least in the USA, yep, a civil engineer designing spacecraft. Analysis is analysis and the mechanical side can be done by aerospace, mechanical, or civil engineering pretty much equally well, you learn most of the job on the job 

  You'll probably be able to find local work for civil, you might have to move for electrical, it depends on what subspecialties you go into and whether you get certified. Here in the USA, not everyone even works in a job where you could become a professional engineer because you have to work with other professional engineers to get them to sign off on you taking the exam. In the state of California where I live, you could actually become a professional engineer without ever going to college, you have to work four more years in the field, but you still have to take the same engineering in training or EIT, and then the subject matter test after you've been working an industry that you need to get sign off for from other PEs 

  Good luck out there, look past college and figure out what your bullseye might look like and then you can try to become the dart that hits it

POST CONTENT:
How do you guys handle teams with unmotivated and unwilling to work teammates? This is the first week of senior year and I'm already freaking out. ┌─ COMMENT ID: ncdi1bt
│  AUTHOR: mrhoa31103
│  DATE: 2025-09-04T19:28:17
│  UPVOTES: 32
└─
  First thing do not freak out. Your pushiness can actually push people to do less. Jointly create an attack plan on the project, get people to buy into a set of assignments (do not start assigning duties like you’re in charge because you’re not unless they agree), set due dates that work for the project. Good luck. 

  If you can get a project manager from huge company as a starting resource all the better since then they can assist getting the plan formulated. They can work the PM toolsbut the teamwill create the plan.

  ┌─ COMMENT ID: ncdin0d

┌─ COMMENT ID: ncdklln
│  AUTHOR: Nunov_DAbov
│  DATE: 2025-09-04T19:41:06
│  UPVOTES: 11
└─
  I taught Senior Design for many years. Your professor needs a process to deal with this because your group is not the only one with the problem and is otherwise powerless to control it. Without a process in place, you all sink because of a deadbeat. Some can actually accomplish negative work.

  I created weekly group effectiveness reports. Each week, each team member distributed 100 points among all the other team members. It became obvious to everyone who was not pulling their weight. Groups that were lazy and just divided points evenly found they had no basis to complain later. Groups that took the process seriously highlighted the slackers because everyone in the group withheld points from them.

  In real life, this is called a self-managed team. Who do you think manages the flight attendants during a flight? The entire team must.

  ┌─ COMMENT ID: ncfrw6u

A good manager sets the overall direction of the team and trusts the team to do tasks in a way that optimizes their performance.

┌─ COMMENT ID: ncei90o
│  AUTHOR: PeanutTheFerret
│  DATE: 2025-09-04T22:19:52
│  UPVOTES: 2
└─
  First of all, I'd encourage you to take a breath. It's your first week of class for the semester. You've got time to figure things out. 

  Based on your post, I would guess that some of your teammates definitely won't be as motivated as you are - but that is OK. Some of your teammates might have other jobs/responsibilities/classes/life that means they can't invest as much as you can into this project. None of that means the project won't get done, or get done well. It just means that you may need to plan accordingly and develop good collaboration skills. 

  Here are some things that help when working with people who are more or less invested than you are on a team: 
  1) clear communication of expectations & timelines. "We need this testing done by this date in order to meet this deadline, will that be possible?" 
  2) understand strengths/weaknesses of your teammates. Person A is great at CAD, but hates writing. Person B feels confident with public speaking/communication and can take lead on presentations/communication. Assigning work that plays to people's strengths (and ideally, doesnt play to weaknesses) can help some. 
  3) be patient. No one wants to work with the person who put themselves in charge unofficially and bosses everyone around. Teamwork is going to be an important skill when you graduate, and you won't always be able to work with people who think exactly like you do. 

  (Also, to be clear, I am not excusing people who dont show up/fulfill the responsibilities they agreed to/otherwise drop the ball. If these things are happening, especially repeatedly, you should talk to your professor.) 

  Good luck! Senior year is stressful, but you're almost across the finish line :)

  I teach in a college, and if I have people not contributing, they get ejected from the team.   So you, as a productive student, tired of carrying others, should contact your instructor and say that you'll be working independently, due to lack of any effort or engagement from your teammates and if that's not okay with the professor, that you'd be willing to meet with a professor and the team to sort this out. Since you probably don't have a contract.

┌─ COMMENT ID: ncesxlx
│  AUTHOR: yakimawashington
│  DATE: 2025-09-04T23:09:34

└─
  Tough love + some actual advice to get through this"

  My dude, chill out. You haven't even started yet and you're already losing your shit. I'm sure you're one of the best and most hardworking students in your class, but you can't just go into this with the mentality:
  How do you guys handle teams with unmotivated and unwilling to work teammates?...if my team doesn't pull their weight then idk what I would do.

  before you all have even begun working on this team together. Your perceived superiority doesn't matter if you can't work well as a team or communicate effectively, and it already sounds like you'll be going into your meetings in panic, resentment, frustration, and dismissiveness towards your team, and then you will very quickly become the person everyone else is complaining about to the prof. You need to go into this open-minded and a willingness to put some trust in your teammates. 
  I didn't get paired up with anyone I actually like working with. 

  You're not entitled to this. In the real world, you won't usually get to pick your team or coworkers. You're in this for the long haul. Treat them with respect. And DO NOT jump to throw your teammates under the bus to the company sponsor anytime something goes wrong. You might think this will help your own image, but I can tell you it absolutely will not. 

  Deal with issues internally, document discussions or issues that arise, and if they persist, have a group meeting with the prof. If you've documented everything clearly (and your prof already knows the students well), this will help get things sorted. This requires a lot of planning and organization. Every meeting, have a word document ready and leave tracking changes on for everyone at all times (google this if you are unfamiliar). Have people add to the shared document so it is visible who made what promises w/what deadlines via tracked changes, then have people add updates to the same document as they make progress. This should be in a shared cloud folder, but also save a copy on your drive regularly in case it ever happens to "disappear". But again, do not plan on doing this just as a way to preplan for throwing your teammates under the bus. Assume the best of them and just use it for record keeping.

  Company sponsors are also aware there can be deadbeat teammates, but it will look significantly better for you if you just do everything you can to mitigate these problems away from the sponsor than including them in your drama, otherwise, like it or not, you will likely come off as someone who can only work well with the right people rather than most people.

TITLE: Estimating heating costs for my recirculating aquaculture system in austria

POST CONTENT:
Hi everyone,

I’m running a small outdoor RAS in Salzburg (Austria) with 4 × 1000 L IBC tanks (2 with fish, 1 with brushes, 1 moving bed with Hel-X). I keep African catfish at ~27 °C.

The setup is insulated:

Tanks are covered on the sides and bottom with 5 cm styrodur,

Top (lid) with 2 cm styrodur,

Water runs through a 19 mm PE pipe (15 m supply + 15 m return) insulated with 19 mm pipe insulation.

Average temperature here is 11.5 °C.

👉 First rough calculation I made:

ΔT = 27 °C − 11.5 °C = 15.5 K

Heat loss per m² at ΔT ≈ 15.5 K is ~0.31 W/m²·K for 5 cm styrodur (sides/bottom) and ~0.78 W/m²·K for 2 cm styrodur (top).

Total exposed tank surface area ≈ 7.5 m² per IBC × 4 tanks = 30 m²

Rough tank heat loss = ~250 W continuous

Piping (30 m total, 19 mm) adds ~15 W

Total heat load ≈ 265 W at 11.5 °C

That equals ~6.36 kWh per day (265 W × 24 h) → if electricity is €0.25/kWh, about €1.59/day, or ~€48/month.
--

Question:
Does this estimate sound realistic? Do you have rules of thumb, corrections, or better calculation methods for RAS heating losses for this setup? I’d love to hear from others who run heated catfish systems outdoors.

Thanks in advance!

TITLE: The two wolves inside me 😛🐺🫠

POST CONTENT:
This honestly isn’t too dramatic because what’s the point in being sad when we can just be BALLERRR 

Anyways I’m an aerospace engineering student, and I’m currently approaching my sophomore year of college. Right now, I’m taking two summer classes: multi variable calculus 1 and linear algebra 1. 

Since starting engineering, it’s def been a journey of immense exploration and discovery, and I’ve realized: engineering is awesome! I truly mean this, every single engineering related class ive taken I’ve loved (except for gen chem. God I hate chem.) and I’ve gotten involved with some hands on work within campus and I LOVED IT. And this upcoming year, I’m looking for much more, and I’m a part of a senior design team. 

The thing that I’m really struggling with is studying. It’s not that I don’t know how. I’ve ALWAYS been a studier; I’ve never been those people who just shows up to a test unprepared. But recently, and honestly this has started since my AP Physics and Calc classes from senior year of high school, I’d often study and still bomb the tests. And naturally, it’s given me pretty shaky confidence. And given the structure of college classes, it’s much harder to get As (esp in engineering), and I’m realizing I want to aim for those more bc I’m thinking about grad school. 

I guess I’m writing all of this to say that I want to start nailing every test and every class. Maybe it’s vain or whatnot, and it may seem like I’m attaching my worth to my academic performance (whoops) but I love the feeling of putting in honest work and getting a result that matches it. Especially bc crazy or not I LIKE studying. I like sitting at my desk and cranking out answers for homework problems and figuring them out. But I get nervous asf for tests, which alters my judgement, and then I get a disappointing score, and then I feel like I didn’t put in enough effort, and feel like I’m lazy, and then I start feeling like I’m not deserving of rest, and yeah it’s just a mess! I especially find myself returning to this mindset recently bc I have two finals for my summer classes next week and one of the classes has ONLY the final as our only test so if I don’t do well on that, it’s actually genuinely over. 

Additionally, I would like some times on distributing your work evenly throughout the week when you have other commitments, such as research, projects, etc. I want to be prepared for my sophomore year and I also want to prioritize having weekends be PURELY for resets and not just squeezing in more hw time 

Anyways! I know I’m not the first person to feel like this so it’s all good at the end of the day!

┌─ COMMENT ID: ncddivh
│  AUTHOR: Silent-Account7422
│  DATE: 2025-09-04T19:04:41
│  UPVOTES: 3
└─
  I work full time and take 12-14 credits per semester as an online student. One Summer I did 9 credits in 8 weeks. The key for me is continuous improvement. Think of your studying like a process you want to optimize. When are you most productive? When is the opportunity cost of your time the smallest? What study methods benefit you the most in terms of hours in, GPA out? Try things, see what works, and always look for ways to iteratively improve your process.

  I get the most done in long study sessions late at night, so I take advantage of weekends when I can stay up till 2 or 3am and sleep in the next day. I tried working in the evenings after work, but I was tired from working, which made me unproductive. I was forgoing family time for little benefit, so I stopped. I don't take notes, since I get better results paying attention to lectures. I always try to learn from the book and practice problems first, then only watch lectures if I'm having trouble. I schedule time off work to take tests, then take a nap after I get off and stay up late studying before taking tests around midnight. I'm in my senior year and currently have a 3.72 GPA.

└─
  A lot of it depends on where you are in your degree. When I was in my freshman and sophomore years I took 9-12 hours no problem. When I got to my Junior year that went down to between 6 and 9 depending on the classes, although I would generally grab an intersession or summer course to get a few extra hours. My last couple of semesters I took 2 classes max, and it was a struggle. Your capstone class is going to require a LOT of time commitment. For us, we were in the lab working 6+ hours at least 3 times a week. Our final paper was like 190 something pages. Weekly updates and meetings and seminars to go to. I don't know how other schools are, or if we just got an extremely difficult project, but it ate up our lives. Moral of the story. Don't get in a hurry if you don't have to, if it takes an extra semester to both graduate and maintain your sanity, then take an extra semester.

┌─ COMMENT ID: nciq5na
│  AUTHOR: thermaldraft
│  DATE: 2025-09-05T13:23:19
│  UPVOTES: 1
└─
  I used to work full time while taking courses, and honestly the sweet spot for me was around 2 classes. I tried going up to 3 once, and it was doable but very exhausting, basically no social life and every bit of free time went into studying or assignments. The biggest thing that helped me manage was planning ahead and being very disciplined with my schedule. I treated school like another job and blocked out specific hours every day for lectures, homework, or projects. I also learned to be realistic, some semesters I scaled back because my workload at the job was heavier, and that balance made it sustainable long term. If you’re thinking of more than 3 courses while working full time, I’d really weigh how demanding each class is and whether your employer is flexible if exams/projects pile up. It’s definitely possible, but pacing yourself might save a lot of stress.

TITLE: Effectiveness of Minoring

POST CONTENT:
If I don’t pursue grad school, should I be worried about employment (especially in this job market?)

I’m a student at Berkeley intending to major in Physics and minor in EECS concentrating more on upper div EE classes. I’m also planning to do engineering ECs like SEB (rocket building team).

On one hand I hear physics majors are employed in all types of jobs, and on the other hand I hear that physics majors have a much harder time even making the job application filter when applying for engineering jobs. Would having a fleshed out minor in engineering and cs with ECs/internships help remediate that?

Should I be worried about employment post-bachelors? Is it really that bad? Calm my worries haha.

TITLE: What’s the correct answer to this interview question?

POST CONTENT:
I recently applied for a technician job at chevron, and they made me take a quiz, that included this question. I think it’s hard to say, becuase it looks like one gear is wider than the other, and they don’t define how much pressure is being applied, which is what threw me off. If they were equal in diameter I know the movement would be none, but the difference threw me off. looking back i think I definitely make a mistake by saying partly up partly down.

┌─ COMMENT ID: nccb16g
│  AUTHOR: polymath_uk
│  DATE: 2025-09-04T14:27:23
│  UPVOTES: 332
└─
  If the gears are driven, the lhs gear will turn faster than the rhs gear. This will cause the rope to be payed out faster from that spool than the takeup in the other. So it will move down.

    This☝🏻but it still gonna go up after the belt on lhs gear comes completely off (reach the end and makes the belt shorter) and if the gears don’t turn the other way, the system will fail at some point

  I would say down, but it’s a bit confusing as to how they want you to treat the connection points of the belt. 

  If we are assuming they are asking generally and we aren’t using the end of the belt as fixed points to that specific part of the pulley, but as a sort of endless belt, then the answer is down.

  If we assume the belt is hard fixed to that one point on the pulley, then it will move downward for a portion of the first rotation and then only upward until the pulley with the weight gets lodged in between the other two…but I don’t think that’s what they’re getting at.

And in reality even if it was a long and finite spooled up belt then it would still go down at first then up when it starts spooling up the other way. Basically the question just needs to add in "at t=0" and all confusion would be gone.

┌─ COMMENT ID: nccay1l
│  AUTHOR: VII-Stardust
│  DATE: 2025-09-04T14:26:31
│  UPVOTES: 51
└─
  Assuming these are equally sized winches with an undefined length of rope, which would be what the image implies;

  The smaller gear meshes with the larger gear, so it is turning faster. Since both winches appear to be the same size, the one that is turning faster would have a greater effect; since that is the one on the left, that means the weight will be lowered.

  ┌─ COMMENT ID: ncccn0x
  │  AUTHOR: Gcarsk
  │  DATE: 2025-09-04T14:43:47
  │  UPVOTES: 4
  └─
    Yup. Left spool would unwind faster than the right spool winds up, because it’s rotating at a faster angular velocity (since it’s the smaller gear). As the belt gets longer, the weight lowers.

    If the gears were the same size, the weight wouldn’t move (besides friction from the belt, but it wouldn’t move vertically in any meaningful way). If the left gear was larger, the weight would be pulled up.

    This. Not ambiguous.

  └─
    Partly up and partly down would obviously mean it goes up for a period then down for a period or vice versa. Which would technically be the case if the belt is fixed to the spools and it reaches the end for the spool on the left. And based on how the diagram is drawn with the belt being black and how we can see the grey color of the top of the spools, it appears this would indeed be what happens with less than a revolution. I would have still answered down myself to be less risky, but others may overanalyze without the question specifying they want it at t=0. The only ones that flunked are the question writers. I remember in engineering school some of the most simple exam questions from some profs. would have a big paragraph explaining all the conditions and assumptions, to the point it almost seemed ridiculous. They clearly had written a question poorly like this one in the past and botched an exam because of it.

┌─ COMMENT ID: ncjh8lq

│  DATE: 2025-09-05T17:20:47
│  UPVOTES: 1
└─
  from my perspective, the LH gear is smaller than RH gear. which means the smaller gear will spin faster than the other. the 'belt' on small gear is unwinding while on the bigger gear it is winding. since LH gear will spin faster, the unwinding action is faster than the winding action, therefore practically the weight will move DOWN.

┌─ COMMENT ID: ncjrob2
│  AUTHOR: CareerOk9462
│  DATE: 2025-09-05T18:25:24
│  UPVOTES: 1
└─
  You have all the information you need.  It indicates that the left gear, source drum, is rotating counter clockwise, the right gear, pull-up drum, is rotating clockwise.  The left gear is rotating more rapidly than the right gear.  The drums are both the same size.  So you are releasing more cable than you are pulling up, so the weight is going down.

  It appears that the drums are the same diameter so the amount of torque being applied to both is the same and in the opposite direction.  But the left gear has the mechanical advantage of the gear ratios.

  Don't overthink it and wonder what happens when you run out of cable, that wasn't the question.

┌─ COMMENT ID: ncccn0x
│  AUTHOR: Gcarsk
│  DATE: 2025-09-04T14:43:47
│  UPVOTES: 4
└─
  Yup. Left spool would unwind faster than the right spool winds up, because it’s rotating at a faster angular velocity (since it’s the smaller gear). As the belt gets longer, the weight lowers.

  If the gears were the same size, the weight wouldn’t move (besides friction from the belt, but it wouldn’t move vertically in any meaningful way). If the left gear was larger, the weight would be pulled up.

└─
  This. Not ambiguous. 

  Gears are meshed, therefore the tips of the gear teeth have the same linear velocity. Different angular speed due to sizes, but the tips of the gear teeth are moving at the same speed. 

  One side is going down at X m/s, and the other side is going down at X m/s. Due to the pulley, the height of the payload does not move.

  Partly up and partly down would obviously mean it goes up for a period then down for a period or vice versa. Which would technically be the case if the belt is fixed to the spools and it reaches the end for the spool on the left. I would have still answered down myself to be less risky, but others may overanalyze without the question specifying they want it at t=0. The only ones that flunked are the question writers. I remember in engineering school some of the most simple exam questions from some profs. would have a big paragraph explaining all the conditions and assumptions, to the point it almost seemed ridiculous. They clearly had written a question poorly like this one in the past and botched an exam because of it.

└─
  The overlap is less than you think beyond introductory classes.

  Physicist do get hired in roles related to instrumentation, semiconductor, optic, radio waves, etc. However, there are also engineering domains not immediately accessible to a generalist/someone not specialized in it. These are the "more interesting" roles in engineering. 

  Also, a subtle difference is, physicists have slightly different way of thinking/approaching problems than engineers.

┌─ COMMENT ID: ncdkfph
│  AUTHOR: Jorlung
│  DATE: 2025-09-04T19:40:18
│  UPVOTES: 5
└─
  As someone that did an Engineering Physics degree, there is really very little overlap (aside from a little bit with EE) after your first year. Taking a bunch of courses in quantum mechanics and particle physics doesn’t do very much to directly help your understanding of how to build a bridge or a car.

  I think engineering majors largely misunderstand a physics degree to just be a more theoretical engineering degree. But ultimately they take an entirely different set of courses that cover topics that are mostly entirely decoupled from the topics you study in engineering (again, aside from some stuff in EE). 

  With that said, it’s not too difficult for physics majors to transition into an engineering masters and then find a job related to their masters. Physics majors are usually able to quickly catch up on the material in an engineering program, but the average physics major just hasn’t looked at this material as part of their program, so that’s why the masters degree is necessary unless they can convincingly demonstrate a sufficient amount of self-study.

└─
  As someone being a TA for physics courses while studying mechanical engineering, there’s a big difference in the advanced courses, especially looking at analytical vs theoretical formulas. There’s also the differing degree requirements due to special engineering accreditation organizations (in the US it is ABET), and specializations (and subspecializations) by degree.

  I can definitely see someone with a specialty in physics that overlaps with the same area in engineering, and has a good background in the applied physics / industry processes (statistics especially) being a good candidate for an engineering role. Likewise, a physics student who did well with waves, optics, and studied the EM spectrum would have useful knowledge for an RF focused role. However, you would have to ask the specific company, as pure physics might or might not be close enough for the role.

┌─ COMMENT ID: ncd7ceh
│  AUTHOR: LitRick6
│  DATE: 2025-09-04T18:30:49
│  UPVOTES: 1
└─
  Its possible. Ive seen people in the sub who said they got engineering jobs with physics degrees. But being possible does not mean its likely. 

  But the overlap of degrees is a lot less than you seem to think it is. There are many specific engineering courses that you are just not going to learn in a physics major. There's going to be more practical stuff in engineering whereas in physics you may learn more theory. 

  Youre luck in finding an engineering job may depend on what types of roles you go for and what experience you have. For example, you might not have as hard of a time getting an engineering position for a research/lab type job but you might struggle getting hands-on or design jobs. 

  But specific experience may also help you. Like doing undergrad research with an engineering professor may help you even more with research/lab engineering roles. For instance, Im an aerospace engineer and AIAA format is common for research papers. I learned AIAA format in my classes but also got extra practice with by doing undergrad research with an aero professor. A physics major, probably isn't learning AIAA format specifically but if you do undergrad research with an aero professor you might learn AIAA.

  For non-research roles, getting some hands-on and design experience would be good. You could try to join clubs/orgs at your university that design and build projects. Understanding non-scientific constraints (ie costs, logistics, etc) is important for engineering solutions and may not be taught in a physics major so practicing that via club/org projects could help. There are also some non-research roles that really dont involve much engineering and just require being able to understand the science and math so a physics major could easily fit that. 

  Assuming youre in the US, you may also want to check what your state's (or any other state you'd want to live in, or provinces if you include Canada) requires for a PE license. I know states can allow engineering technicians/technologist to become licensed engineers but idk if they let physics majors do it to or not. 

  All that said, you could also still be shit out of luck. At my aerospace company, you would outright be barred from applying to any engineering job if you had a physics degree. We require an ABET accredited engineering degree. TBH I dont think its so much that a physics major couldn't learn everything they need to for the job, but moreso the legal department of companies not wanting to have to justify an employees credentials when we are working on safety critical items and something bad could happen if there's any issues.

TITLE: What prestige level should I target for an MS in engineering?

POST CONTENT:
I’m planning to apply for MS programs in engineering and trying to figure out where I realistically fit in terms of prestige level.

Background: I just finished undergrad at Wake Forest with a B.S. in Engineering (electrical & computer concentration) and minors in math + CS. GPA is 3.95. I’ve done a lot of math/CS-heavy coursework plus some projects — things like machine learning (CNNs, a custom loss function for eye-tracking) and a hardware project creating variable bike resistance for dialysis patients. No publications yet, though I might have a preprint ready before applications.

Given that, what tier of programs do you think I should realistically be targeting prestige-wise — the absolute top, the next tier down, or more like strong-but-less-famous programs?

└─
  A big state university with a good engineering program and lots of companies around the area. There might be some edges to doing an engineering MS at Harvard, like better connections, professors, etc., but it's not worth paying an extra 30k in tuition every year in my opinion. A land grant research university will have top tier research and industry connections just like any Ivy League.

    └─
      I think you can get into most masters programs, even top 10, with a GPA like that. Problem is, many masters programs in the US have become cash grabs, have accepted more people with lesser qualifications, and have diluted their prestige by their own hands. In my own uni (big state uni) graduate population almost quadrupled in the last 10 years. There's constant complaint from CS MS students about not being able to enroll in classes because there's no more room but the department keep taking on more students. That's why I suggested to pay as little as possible, if the end goal is to find decent employment after graduation.

┌─ COMMENT ID: ncberzu

│  DATE: 2025-09-04T09:32:08

└─
  With no publications and no lab/research experience but a high GPA you can still target top 30 programs easily (top 5 might not be as likely with no publications or dedicated research experience but at that point it’s kinda splitting hairs in terms of prestige) but you’ll still have to beef your app as much as you can with good letters of recommendations from professors who can attest to your projects. You really just wanna demonstrate you can handle rigorous academics and rigorous projects/research.

  The other person is right too. Since most masters aren’t funded without student secured scholarships and fellowships so you need to go where’s most affordable and has the most opportunity for these kinds of funding. Connections also matter more than prestige (although prestige kinda automatically comes with connections but the opposite of not having connections in a smaller program isn’t necessarily true). 

  Location also matters, you’ll be there for 2 years so don’t pick a school in an area you hate.

      I’m approaching this from a PhD apps perspective since that’s what I’m doing right now but masters programs typically have less of a “high bar” for entry so regardless you still have a really good shot at good programs I would say. 

      My strategy is to have different levels of schools that I’m applying to, so I have a few lower ranked programs, several mid tier (my target schools that I could reasonably expect to get admitted to), and one or two high tie schools almost as a Hail Mary lmao.

┌─ COMMENT ID: ncboasj
│  AUTHOR: ice0rb

│  UPVOTES: 2
└─
  It depends on your goals really?

  Top 1% in your lifetime? Worth it to try to get an Ivy-level. (not necessarily Ivy since they're not all great at engineering)

  Just want a good job? Yes, big state school works.

  I don't want to be class blind here so, Ivy's have higher tuition-- yes, but they also connect you with people who have more money (i.e. wealthy people) which help propel you when say, you want an investment in a startup you made, or want to find people who enjoy travelling more (idfk). I say this as someone who got into several Ivy for grad school and went to a big state school. Big state school kids are interested in landing solid, stable jobs. Ivy kids (not all, be tend to have more of) are more-so concerned with status climbing, starting their own companies, etc. things normal people can't really concern themselves because if they had no job they wouldn't be able to pay the bills.

TITLE: Sanity check on my fail-safe pneumatic release (human-powered submarine)

POST CONTENT:
I’m on a student team representing Singapore at EISR. We’re building a fail-safe buoy release for our human-powered submarine: if the pilot lets go (unconscious/loss of control), the system automatically vents and a single-acting cylinder retracts to release the buoy. Components must be from SMC Singapore (except the scuba bits), and we operate around 5–6 m depth.

Operating principle (simple flow)
Tank + scuba first stage → about 7 bar intermediate pressure (ambient-compensated).
SMC mini-reg (ARJ210-M5G) regulates to around 5–6 bar.
SMC hand lever 3/2 NC, spring return (VHL212S-02) is the dead-man.
Lever held: P→A sends air to the cylinder (buoy held).
Lever released / air lost: A→EA vents; spring retracts cylinder (buoy releases).
Speed control: one AS1201F-M5-06A at the cylinder port.

Constraints (non-negotiable)
 • Depth: 5–6 m max, wet use; rinse after dives.
 • Air source: Yoke first stage on a small pony (or Pro DIN/K with yoke insert). IP set ≈ 7 bar (95–100 psi).
 • Pneumatics brand: SMC Singapore only (valves, reg, fittings, tube).
 • Mini-reg: SMC ARJ210-M5G (inlet ≤ 8 bar; set to ~5–6 bar).
 • Dead-man: SMC VHL212S-02 (3/2 NC, spring return).
 • Actuator: SMC CJ2R16-xx single-acting, spring return.
 • Fittings/tube: 6 mm OD (TU0604), KQ2 push-ins.
 • First-stage LP port: 3/8-24 UNF (F) → adapter 3/8-24 UNF (M) → 1/8-NPT (F) → 6 mm → 1/8-NPT (M) push-in.

Just want to ask if this is even workable underwater for my safety system and how would i waterproof it if theres a need.

└─
  No you won’t be locked out of your desired degree. Everyone takes this placement test, to my knowledge. For reading, writing, and math. They need to gauge how well you are at the subject to match the college level class equivalent as to not throw you to the wolves. 

  Now, if you haven’t learned what ideally you should have - that’s bad news. That’s all the math placement test is. 

  Good thing is this test isn’t pass or fail, just sees what you know. If you score less than the required minimum, you will be required to take an intro to whatever college math course needed before you can start actual college level maths. Or you take the test again till pass. So this may push you back a semester.

  My advice to you is get a tutor asap to teach you at least 30-50% of algebra and precal so your score is mid range decent. I wouldn’t strive for learning it all in your case, just make peace with it. 

  I recently had to take this test after being away from math for 9 years…i had always put it off but finally decided i needed to finish my degree involving math. Studied a bit from Jan til August, minimum score in my state is 950. First try i got a 938! 2nd try 941 till eventually 951. I had some fantastic HS math teachers who i thank for teaching me their tricks and methods that came rushing back in after so many years. Good luck! :)

┌─ COMMENT ID: ncbniri
│  AUTHOR: chisholmdale
│  DATE: 2025-09-04T10:41:47
│  UPVOTES: 2
└─
  A few thoughts, in random order: 
  The people who matter will form their judgements on more than superficial name-recognition. 
  Depending on how you structure your departmental electives, UofM may give better preparation for follow-on study at the PhD level. But you probably need to have that as a definite goal, not just "Some day I might go for a PhD.". 
  What were your academic weaknesses in High School? It used to be that some students who went to MTU with a C-average in High School - and couldn't get admitted to UofM - did well at Tech because their strengths were not in the subjects which dominated High School curricula.
  Ann Arbor will probably present more distractions, and temptations to neglect your studies, than Houghton. 
  It's interesting that you describe MTU as "isolated". (Some students go there because it's as far away from home as they can get, but have the advantage of in-state tuition.) "Isolation" means many different things to different people. For some, the remoteness encourages growth in self-sufficiency and independence - which may be either good or bad, depending on your core values. For others, it encourages psychological withdrawal and cultural insularity. No, you can't zip home on a weekend and have mom do a month's worth of laundry for you. Likewise, it's unlikely that a parent will drop in - either announced, or unannounced - to advise you on your study habits, your dating life, or any other topic on their mind.

└─
  Michigan tech produces fine engineers. 

  University of Michigan (I assume Ann Arbor) is a great school but at the end of the day you really need to consider if the differences between UofM and MT are worth the transfer. I do think it is worth transferring to UofM if and only if you are planning on going to graduate school. UofM has a much more fleshed out research program and larger labs as a result. If you aren't planning on going off to graduate school, I don't think there is going to be much of a difference between MT and UofM. 

  To add to that, if you're happy at MT, just stay there. To be honest, I would hate to attend Michigan Tech because well, it's a small isolated school. But if that's your jam, just stay there. Caveat, I didn't attend UofM and I'm extrapolating from UIUC (another big10 school). But large campus, large student body. Lots of activities to do. I personally enjoyed going to a large state university but you can feel invisible at times. If you are really happy with the student life at MT, I would stay there. I just know personally that if I went to MT, I might have gone insane with what I've heard about that school.

          There’s going to be strong opinions against it from a lot of very smart people who make very good points. My experience with it is more from a pragmatic frame of reference than an academic/intellectual one. 

          I’m a returning learner who has limited time due to a 50-60 hour work week and have family life obligations. I don’t have lots of time to be searching for answers like I would if I was full time college student. I have to find ways to streamline work, school and family as best as possible. 

          My compromise is that I will use AI if I cannot find an immediate resource within a reasonable amount of time. When I use it, I refuse to use it in a way that compromises my ability to actually retain critical information. I also come from a corporate background where your method of completion isn’t as important as a finished product that has the same quality. I’m trying to upskill inside an industry where I have a good bit of experience so I don’t need the same thing most college students need from classes. 

          Regardless, make sure you’re actually learning how the mechanics of whatever you’re learning works. It’s hard to go back later and learn again

  └─
    There’s going to be strong opinions against it from a lot of very smart people who make very good points. My experience with it is more from a pragmatic frame of reference than an academic/intellectual one. 

    I’m a returning learner who has limited time due to a 50-60 hour work week and have family life obligations. I don’t have lots of time to be searching for answers like I would if I was full time college student. I have to find ways to streamline work, school and family as best as possible. 

    My compromise is that I will use AI if I cannot find an immediate resource within a reasonable amount of time. When I use it, I refuse to use it in a way that compromises my ability to actually retain critical information. I also come from a corporate background where your method of completion isn’t as important as a finished product that has the same quality. I’m trying to upskill inside an industry where I have a good bit of experience so I don’t need the same thing most college students need from classes. 

    Regardless, make sure you’re actually learning how the mechanics of whatever you’re learning works. It’s hard to go back later and learn again

        There’s going to be strong opinions against it from a lot of very smart people who make very good points. My experience with it is more from a pragmatic frame of reference than an academic/intellectual one. 

        I’m a returning learner who has limited time due to a 50-60 hour work week and have family life obligations. I don’t have lots of time to be searching for answers like I would if I was full time college student. I have to find ways to streamline work, school and family as best as possible. 

        My compromise is that I will use AI if I cannot find an immediate resource within a reasonable amount of time. When I use it, I refuse to use it in a way that compromises my ability to actually retain critical information. I also come from a corporate background where your method of completion isn’t as important as a finished product that has the same quality. I’m trying to upskill inside an industry where I have a good bit of experience so I don’t need the same thing most college students need from classes. 

        Regardless, make sure you’re actually learning how the mechanics of whatever you’re learning works. It’s hard to go back later and learn again

    └─
      There’s going to be strong opinions against it from a lot of very smart people who make very good points. My experience with it is more from a pragmatic frame of reference than an academic/intellectual one. 

      I’m a returning learner who has limited time due to a 50-60 hour work week and have family life obligations. I don’t have lots of time to be searching for answers like I would if I was full time college student. I have to find ways to streamline work, school and family as best as possible. 

      My compromise is that I will use AI if I cannot find an immediate resource within a reasonable amount of time. When I use it, I refuse to use it in a way that compromises my ability to actually retain critical information. I also come from a corporate background where your method of completion isn’t as important as a finished product that has the same quality. I’m trying to upskill inside an industry where I have a good bit of experience so I don’t need the same thing most college students need from classes. 

      Regardless, make sure you’re actually learning how the mechanics of whatever you’re learning works. It’s hard to go back later and learn again

    └─
      There’s going to be strong opinions against it from a lot of very smart people who make very good points. My experience with it is more from a pragmatic frame of reference than an academic/intellectual one. 

      I’m a returning learner who has limited time due to a 50-60 hour work week and have family life obligations. I don’t have lots of time to be searching for answers like I would if I was full time college student. I have to find ways to streamline work, school and family as best as possible. 

      My compromise is that I will use AI if I cannot find an immediate resource within a reasonable amount of time. When I use it, I refuse to use it in a way that compromises my ability to actually retain critical information. I also come from a corporate background where your method of completion isn’t as important as a finished product that has the same quality. I’m trying to upskill inside an industry where I have a good bit of experience so I don’t need the same thing most college students need from classes. 

      Regardless, make sure you’re actually learning how the mechanics of whatever you’re learning works. It’s hard to go back later and learn again

  ┌─ COMMENT ID: ncaxpd9
  │  AUTHOR: Substantial_Brain917
  │  DATE: 2025-09-04T07:37:46
  │  UPVOTES: 2
  └─
    There’s going to be strong opinions against it from a lot of very smart people who make very good points. My experience with it is more from a pragmatic frame of reference than an academic/intellectual one. 

    I’m a returning learner who has limited time due to a 50-60 hour work week and have family life obligations. I don’t have lots of time to be searching for answers like I would if I was full time college student. I have to find ways to streamline work, school and family as best as possible. 

    My compromise is that I will use AI if I cannot find an immediate resource within a reasonable amount of time. When I use it, I refuse to use it in a way that compromises my ability to actually retain critical information. I also come from a corporate background where your method of completion isn’t as important as a finished product that has the same quality. I’m trying to upskill inside an industry where I have a good bit of experience so I don’t need the same thing most college students need from classes. 

    Regardless, make sure you’re actually learning how the mechanics of whatever you’re learning works. It’s hard to go back later and learn again

    I use AI all the time it's a great tool to help you learn. Other people who say don't use it probably don't use it so they don't know.

    When people say to use AI they don't mean to ask it to do it all for you, what they mean is let it see where you lack understanding and let it help bridge the gaps. At least that's what I do and it's helped me perform very well vs not using it.
